name: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type 1 (HSAN1)

clinicalPearls: The commonest dominantly inherited sensory neuropathy, most often caused by variants in SPTLC1 (and SPTLC2) encoding subunits of serine palmitoyltransferase, the rate-limiting enzyme of sphingolipid synthesis.
Typical onset is in the second to fourth decade with distal sensory loss in the feet, predominantly affecting pain and temperature sensation early.
Painless injuries lead to recurrent foot ulceration, poor healing, osteomyelitis, Charcot joints and acro-mutilation with distal amputations.
Paradoxically, many patients experience prominent lancinating or burning neuropathic pain despite marked sensory loss.
Autonomic features (distal anhidrosis) are usually milder than in other HSAN subtypes, and sensorineural hearing loss occurs in some families.
The mechanism is a toxic gain of function: mutant serine palmitoyltransferase produces neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids (deoxysphinganine) rather than a simple loss of enzyme activity.
Oral L-serine supplementation is under investigation as a substrate-based strategy to lower deoxysphingolipid production and is a distinctive management consideration for this subtype.
Meticulous foot care, protective footwear and prompt treatment of injuries are the cornerstone of preventing mutilating complications.
reference.pathophysiology: HSAN1 most commonly arises from missense variants in SPTLC1 or SPTLC2, the catalytic subunits of serine palmitoyltransferase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme in de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis, which normally condenses serine with palmitoyl-CoA. The disease-causing variants alter substrate specificity so the enzyme also uses alanine and glycine, generating atypical 1-deoxysphingolipids that cannot be converted to complex sphingolipids or normally degraded. These deoxysphingolipids accumulate and are neurotoxic to sensory and autonomic neurons, disrupting the cytoskeleton, mitochondrial function and neurite integrity, with a length-dependent predilection that explains the distal-to-proximal, lower-limb-first pattern of degeneration. The result is a dying-back axonopathy affecting predominantly small myelinated and unmyelinated fibres, producing early loss of pain and temperature sensation, later large-fibre involvement, and the characteristic combination of profound sensory loss with neuropathic pain. Because the defect is a toxic gain of function driven by aberrant substrate use, dietary L-serine can competitively favour the normal reaction and reduce deoxysphingolipid formation, providing a mechanistic rationale for supplementation.
additionalDifferentials: Other HSAN subtypes (HSAN2 recessive; HSAN3/familial dysautonomia; HSAN4 and HSAN5 with congenital insensitivity to pain)
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, especially forms with sensory predominance
Diabetic and other metabolic sensory neuropathies with foot ulceration
Tabes dorsalis and other causes of sensory ataxia with neuropathic joints
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and quantitative sensory testing showing a length-dependent sensory-predominant axonal neuropathy
Targeted genetic testing of SPTLC1/SPTLC2 and an HSAN/inherited neuropathy gene panel
Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density to assess small-fibre loss
Autonomic function testing including sudomotor assessment
Foot radiographs and imaging for osteomyelitis or Charcot neuroarthropathy
redFlags: Non-healing or deep foot ulcers with signs of osteomyelitis
Acute red, warm, swollen foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy
Rapidly progressive tissue loss or acro-mutilation
New or worsening sensorineural hearing loss
Severe intractable neuropathic pain limiting function
reference.prognosis: HSAN1 is slowly progressive over decades; lifespan is usually preserved but morbidity is substantial from recurrent ulceration, infection and amputation. Diligent preventive foot care markedly reduces mutilating complications, and substrate-based therapy is an area of active investigation.
pitfalls: Attributing painless foot ulceration to diabetes and missing an inherited neuropathy in a suggestive family history
Assuming profound sensory loss excludes significant neuropathic pain
Delaying protective foot-care measures until after ulceration develops
Regarding the enzyme defect as simple loss of function rather than a toxic gain of function, which misframes therapy
references: Standard peripheral neuropathy and neurogenetics textbooks
Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy review literature (source-neutral)
management: Institute meticulous preventive foot care with daily inspection, protective well-fitting footwear, offloading, prompt wound treatment and regular podiatry to avoid painless injury
Treat foot ulceration, osteomyelitis and Charcot neuroarthropathy aggressively with orthopaedic and surgical input to limit acro-mutilation and amputation
Manage the lancinating and burning neuropathic pain with agents such as gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants or duloxetine
Consider substrate-based therapy with oral L-serine supplementation, which lowers production of the neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids and is under active investigation
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, podiatry, orthopaedics, pain and rehabilitation services, and screen for and manage sensorineural hearing loss
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant SPTLC1/SPTLC2 inheritance with family testing
